title: Solid-state reaction synthesis of superconducting refractory-metal germanides for Ge/SiGe quantum devices
authors: Sebastiaan R. Roelofs, Jan Cornelis Wolff, Nick van Loo, Karina L. Hudson, Giordano Scappucci, Greg P. Mazur
abstract: Solid-phase reactions offer a route to integrate superconductors into Ge/SiGe heterostructures, but forming high-quality superconducting layers near the buried Ge quantum well remains challenging. We investigate reactions of V, Ta, and Nb with elemental Ge and with the Si$_{0.2}$Ge$_{0.8}$ barrier of Ge/SiGe heterostructures at processing temperatures of 365-390 $^\circ$C. Cross-sectional electron microscopy and low-temperature electrical transport show that deposition on Ge at 390 $^\circ$C, in which approximately 2 nm metal increments are separated by growth stops for in-situ annealing, produces reactions throughout the deposited films and superconducting transitions at approximately 0.14 K for V-Ge, 2.1 K for Ta-Ge, and 2.8 K for Nb-Ge. The Nb-Ge layer has an out-of-plane critical field of approximately 0.8 T at 2.1 K. In the heterostructure samples, intermixing is confined to regions approximately 5-12 nm thick near the metal-SiGe interface, leaving a substantial residual metal layer. Microscopy and transport together suggest that this residual film dominates the measured superconducting response. These results establish low-temperature formation of superconducting refractory-metal-Ge layers while identifying the limited interfacial reaction as the principal obstacle to extending this approach toward the buried quantum well.
summary: This work reports on synthesizing superconducting refractory-metal germanides on Ge/SiGe heterostructures using low-temperature solid-state reactions. While superconductivity is achieved on elemental Ge, the reaction process is significantly hindered by the SiGe alloy barrier, limiting the superconducting layer formation to the immediate interface rather than the buried quantum well. This identifies interfacial reaction kinetics as the primary hurdle for integrating superconductors into these quantum devices.
main_problem: The primary challenge is developing a reliable, low-temperature method to integrate superconducting refractory-metal germanides into Ge/SiGe heterostructures for use in quantum devices, especially near a buried quantum well.
main_result: Low-temperature solid-state reactions successfully form superconducting germanides (e.g., Nb-Ge) on elemental Ge, but the reaction kinetics are severely limited when crossing the SiGe alloy barrier, which is the main obstacle for device integration.
method: The study employs solid-state reaction synthesis using V, Ta, and Nb deposited onto Ge/SiGe structures, followed by characterization using cross-sectional electron microscopy and low-temperature electrical transport measurements.
model_or_system: The physical system is planar Ge/SiGe heterostructures, which are promising platforms for quantum devices. Superconductivity is induced by forming refractory-metal germanides (V, Ta, Nb) through controlled solid-phase reactions.
key_observables: Superconducting critical temperatures ($T_c$) (e.g., 2.8 K for Nb-Ge), out-of-plane critical fields ($B_c$), and the thickness/nature of the interfacial reaction layer (5-12 nm).
important_parameters: Processing temperatures ($365–390^\circ	ext{C}$), the composition of the barrier ($	ext{Si}_{0.2}	ext{Ge}_{0.8}$), and the metal used (V, Ta, Nb).
main_assumptions: The superconducting response in the heterostructure is dominated by the thin reacted film at the metal-SiGe interface, not the buried quantum well.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the preparation and characterization of V, Ta, and Nb reactions on both bulk Ge and Ge/SiGe structures, showing depth profiles of the resulting reaction layers.
paper_structure: The paper systematically investigates the synthesis of superconducting germanides on elemental Ge first, establishing feasibility, and then applies this to the more complex Ge/SiGe heterostructure, where the limitations of the interfacial reaction kinetics are identified.
why_interesting: While the focus is on materials synthesis rather than fundamental quantum dynamics, the successful creation of superconducting interfaces on semiconductor platforms is crucial for realizing superconducting qubits or quantum interconnects, linking condensed matter physics to quantum information.
